prompt: A detune control applies the same positive cents offset to a bass note and a high note. Which result should you expect?

options.text: The same added hertz on both notes
options.explanation: Cents describe a frequency ratio, rather than an absolute hertz offset.

options.text: The same upward musical interval on both notes
options.explanation: Correct. Cents divide equal-tempered pitch intervals uniformly.

options.text: The bass note must move by more hertz
options.explanation: For the same ratio, the higher starting frequency has the larger absolute hertz change.

options.text: Only the high note changes because cents are for treble
options.explanation: Cents are usable at any positive frequency.

workedExample: A cent is one hundredth of a semitone. The same cents setting therefore makes the same musical interval on both notes; it multiplies both frequencies by the same ratio.

prompt: A tuner reports a fractional note number slightly below 68. What should its nearest-note and detune display show?

options.text: Note 69, because every fraction rounds upward
options.explanation: Choose the nearest whole note rather than always rounding up.

options.text: Note 67, because the reading is below 68
options.explanation: Being slightly below 68 still leaves it much closer to 68 than 67.
Correct. The nearest whole note is 68 and the measured pitch lies below it.
The sign is reversed: a pitch below its reference note is flat.

workedExample: Find the nearest whole note number first. Then keep the signed fractional difference from that note. A small negative difference means slightly flat, rather than a whole note lower.

prompt: Two close oscillators use a fixed cents detune. You play the same patch one octave higher. What happens to the beat rate?

options.explanation: Correct. Both frequencies double, so their hertz difference doubles too.

options.text: It stays fixed because the cents value is unchanged
options.explanation: The musical interval stays fixed; its hertz difference grows with the starting frequency.
A higher register enlarges, rather than reduces, the hertz separation for the same ratio.
Close tones still drift in and out of phase when raised together.

workedExample: Beating follows the hertz difference between close tones. Cents set a ratio. Raising both tones an octave doubles their frequencies and their separation, so the wobble becomes twice as fast.
